content: The American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) is an organization that certifies physicians who specialize in internal medicine and its subspecialties. Over 180,000 physicians in the United States are ABIM-certified, which accounts for approximately one-third of all practicing physicians in the country. The current president and CEO of ABIM is Christine K. Cassel, MD. ABIM was established in 1936, and its certifications are globally recognized as a hallmark of high physician competence. Earning an ABIM certification signifies that a physician has undergone rigorous training and has been systematically evaluated for their expertise. ABIM is one of 24 certifying boards recognized by the American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) and focuses on the specialty of internal medicine. Physicians can obtain ABIM certification after successfully completing residency or fellowship training and passing a secure examination that assesses their medical knowledge. Board certification is widely regarded as a standard of excellence in the medical field. Many hospitals require internists to be board-certified to grant admitting privileges, and numerous health plans mandate certification for contracting or eligibility in select networks. Since 1990, ABIM certifications have been time-limited to ten years and must be renewed through the Maintenance of Certification (MOC) program. The MOC program consists of four key components: 1. Verification of Credentials: Physicians must hold a valid, unrestricted medical license to practice. Any action against a license undermines the fundamental professional credential required for certification. 2. Self-Evaluation of Medical Knowledge: Physicians engage in open-book knowledge assessments developed by ABIM or other organizations to evaluate their clinical knowledge in specific fields. These assessments not only stimulate learning but also require documentation of that learning. Given the rapid evolution of medical knowledge and technology, it is essential for physicians to stay current. 3. Self-Evaluation of Practice Performance: Physicians utilize ABIM’s Practice Improvement Modules (PIMs) to assess their clinical performance in areas relevant to their practice. This process involves comparing their performance to established clinical guidelines, creating a plan to improve key aspects of their practice, and evaluating the impact of those improvements. This self-assessment helps physicians recognize that the quality of care they provide may not always meet their expectations and emphasizes the importance of measurement and improvement as integral parts of medical practice, rather than externally imposed requirements. 4. Secure Examination: Physicians are required to pass a closed-book, proctored, computer-based examination. This exam includes 180 pre-tested questions designed to simulate real-world clinical scenarios, allowing for the evaluation of critical aspects of clinical knowledge and judgment. The exam assesses not only what physicians know but also how they apply their knowledge to promote health, diagnose conditions, and treat illnesses effectively and efficiently.
